Team 8 – People and HR Analytics · BANA Team Project, PGDM BA 2026

**D4 Note: Using machine learning to understand employee satisfaction**

Members: K Krishnakanth Maheedhar, Irene Roby, Nirshitha Vijaya Kumar, Shirley Dutta, Shashanki Shikha, Shradha Shruti

**1\. The problem in simple words**

HR wants to know **which things at work go together with low job satisfaction, and which groups of employees need attention first.** We use the IBM HR Analytics dataset from Kaggle (1,470 simulated employees, 35 columns, no missing values or duplicate rows). The file has no developer role, so we talk about **employees**, not developers. Everything below shows patterns, not proof of cause.

**2\. Why these two methods**

- **Decision Tree** – asks a chain of yes/no questions (for example "works overtime?") and ends with a guess: Low or High satisfaction. A manager can read the rules, so it shows which work factors go with low satisfaction.
- **K-Means** – sorts employees into groups of similar people (by pay, level, years at work and workplace ratings). We do not tell it who is satisfied. It lets HR plan one action for each group.

**3\. How we set it up**

- **Target:** satisfaction score 1–2 = Low, 3–4 = High. Low employees: 569 (38.7%); High: 901 (61.3%). Because Low is the smaller group, we look at how many Low employees the tree finds (recall) and not accuracy alone.
- **Left out of the models:** the satisfaction score itself, Attrition, the ID and constant columns, the three pay-rate columns (DailyRate, HourlyRate, MonthlyRate – weak link to income), and **Age, Gender and Marital Status** (used only to check fairness). The tree used 23 fields.
- **Fair test:** 1,176 employees to train, 294 kept hidden to test (80/20 split, seed 42, so results repeat). The tree's size (depth 2, at least 40 employees per final box) was chosen using the training part only.

**4\. Decision Tree results**

| **Measure (294 hidden test employees)** | **Result**     | **In plain words**                                                                    |
| --------------------------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Test accuracy                           | 46.3%          | Share guessed correctly. Always saying "High" would score 61.2%.                      |
| Balanced accuracy                       | 50.5%          | Average of the Low and High hit rates; 50% is the same as guessing.                   |
| Recall for Low                          | 69.3%          | The tree found 79 of the 114 truly Low employees.                                     |
| Precision for Low                       | 39.1%          | Of 202 employees flagged Low, 79 really are Low.                                      |
| Train vs test accuracy                  | 52.1% vs 46.3% | Gap of 5.9 points. Both are low, so the tree is not memorising; it is finding little. |
| 5-fold cross-check                      | 53.1% ± 5.5%   | Repeated testing inside the training data gives the same weak picture.                |

**What the tree found:** it used only three fields: **number of companies worked at before (37%), education field (32%) and distance from home (31%)**. The rules are: employees who worked at 3 or fewer companies are predicted Low unless their education field is Life Sciences; employees with more than 3 previous companies are predicted Low unless they live within about 1 unit of work. These are patterns in this data, not reasons that cause low satisfaction. No tenure field appears, so the age-proxy risk named in D2 is not triggered here.

**How reliable is it? Not reliable.** Accuracy (46.3%) is below the 61.2% you get by always guessing High. Balanced accuracy is 50.5%, and precision for Low (39.1%) equals the share of Low employees in the test set (38.8%), so the tree's "Low" flag is no better than picking people at random. Its high recall comes from flagging 202 of 294 employees as Low. The cross-check agrees, and a deeper tree did not score better in training-data cross-validation. **In plain words: the fields in this dataset do not predict job satisfaction.** This fits a simulated dataset where satisfaction scores were not generated from the other fields. The tree should not be used to screen or label anyone.

**Fairness check:** the tree is equally weak for every group, but its recall for Low differs by age. Recall for Low: Female 68.4%, Male 66.3% (gap 2.1 points, within our 10-point limit); Under 30 76.7%, 30–44 62.4%, 45 and over 69.0% (gap 14.3 points between Under 30 and 30–44, **above** our 10-point review limit). Every group has at least 126 Low employees, so none is too small to compare. Because the tree is not predictive, the age gap mostly shows the tree flags young employees as Low more often.

| **Group**   | **Employees** | **Low employees** | **Accuracy** | **Recall (Low)** | **Precision (Low)** |
| ----------- | ------------- | ----------------- | ------------ | ---------------- | ------------------- |
| Female      | 588           | 237               | 48.5%        | 68.4%            | 41.5%               |
| Male        | 882           | 332               | 47.6%        | 66.3%            | 38.6%               |
| Under 30    | 326           | 129               | 49.7%        | 76.7%            | 42.5%               |
| 30–44       | 830           | 314               | 46.9%        | 62.4%            | 37.8%               |
| 45 and over | 314           | 126               | 49.0%        | 69.0%            | 41.8%               |

**5\. K-Means results**

We tried 2 to 6 groups (Figure 2). Two groups score best (silhouette 0.24) but only split junior from senior staff, which is too broad to act on, so we picked the best score from 3 groups upward: **3 groups, silhouette 0.17**. This is below about 0.25, so the groups overlap: they are a convenient grouping by career stage, not sharply separate types.

| **Group** | **Employees** | **Median income** | **Job level** | **Years at company** | **Years since promotion** | **% High satisfaction** |
| --------- | ------------- | ----------------- | ------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| S1        | 765 (52%)     | 3,204             | 1.4           | 3.3                  | 0.7                       | 61%                     |
| S2        | 537 (37%)     | 6,582             | 2.5           | 8.4                  | 2.6                       | 63%                     |
| S3        | 168 (11%)     | 15,140            | 3.8           | 19.6                 | 7.4                       | 57%                     |

Satisfaction was not used to make the groups. Afterwards, High satisfaction runs from 57% (S3) to 63% (S2), against 61% company-wide. This difference is **not statistically reliable** (chi-square p = 0.43, Cramér's V = 0.03), so the groups describe career stage more than satisfaction. Overtime (27–29%) and work-life balance (about 2.7–2.8) are almost the same in all three.

**One action per group:**

- **S1 – early-career, lowest pay and level, newest to the company (52% of staff):** strengthen onboarding, mentoring and early training.
- **S2 – mid-career (37%):** satisfaction is the highest (63%) but close to average; maintain current practice and use career-path talks as years in role grow.
- **S3 – senior, highest pay and level, longest since promotion (7.4 years on average):** review promotion timing and retention or succession plans; its satisfaction share is lowest (57%), but the gap is small, so treat it as a place to ask questions, not as a finding.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

_Figure 2. Silhouette score for 2 to 6 groups; the dashed line marks the chosen 3._

**6\. What this means for HR**

- **Decision supported:** where HR should spend limited time first. The K-Means groups give a plain way to split the workforce by career stage and plan one action each. The tree does **not** give HR a usable way to find unsatisfied employees from these fields.
- **What changes:** HR should not rely on the profile fields in this file to predict satisfaction. Satisfaction needs to be measured directly (pulse surveys, stay interviews), starting with S3 and S1, and then tested again to see whether the actions help.
- **Limits:** simulated single-snapshot data, three departments, no developer role; self-reported 1–4 scores; patterns, not causes; a depth-2 tree is simple on purpose; K-Means groups depend on the columns and number of groups chosen. Next step for D5: test a second method such as logistic regression to confirm the weak signal, and keep the fairness check.

References: Pavan Subhash, IBM HR Analytics Employee Attrition and Performance \[dataset\], Kaggle; Provost & Fawcett (2013), Data Science for Business; Chapman et al. (2000), CRISP-DM 1.0; Mehrabi et al. (2021), A survey on bias and fairness in machine learning.
